pairs.title: Freezer plug
pairs.version_a: Dana volunteers at a community hall. On Saturday morning she walks past a freezer holding a rival caterer's ice cream cakes, which are meant for a wedding that afternoon. She wants the cakes to melt so the wedding party will hire her instead. She pulls the freezer's plug from the wall and walks on. By noon the cakes have melted, and the caterer has to refund the wedding party.
pairs.version_b: Dana volunteers at a community hall. On Saturday morning she walks past a freezer holding a rival caterer's ice cream cakes, which are meant for a wedding that afternoon. She needs the socket for her vacuum cleaner and does not notice the freezer is running. She pulls the freezer's plug from the wall and walks on. By noon the cakes have melted, and the caterer has to refund the wedding party.
pairs.intended_difference: Dana pulls the plug on purpose to ruin the cakes (A) versus by mistake while wanting a socket (B); action and outcome are the same.
pairs.judgment_question: How much does Dana deserve to be criticized for what happened to the cakes?
pairs.comprehension_question: What did Dana want when she pulled the plug?
pairs.option_b: A socket for her vacuum cleaner
pairs.option_c: To move the freezer to another room
pairs.prediction_rationale: Deliberate sabotage versus an innocent mistake with identical outcomes should produce a very large blame gap, even among AI readers.
pairs.originality_note: Original setting (hall freezer, rival caterer); not a re-skin of a standard intent/accident case such as the poisoned-coffee or Knobe-style vignettes.

pairs.title: Greenhouse heater
pairs.version_a: Marcus is looking after his neighbor's greenhouse for the weekend. The neighbor is entering her tomato seedlings in a regional contest against Marcus's own. Marcus knows tonight's frost will kill the seedlings unless the heater runs, and he wants them to die so his own will win. The heater is running, and Marcus flips its switch to off. He goes home. The frost kills every seedling overnight.
pairs.version_b: Marcus is looking after his neighbor's greenhouse for the weekend. The neighbor is entering her tomato seedlings in a regional contest against Marcus's own. Marcus knows tonight's frost will kill the seedlings unless the heater runs, and he wants them to die so his own will win. The heater has just switched itself off, and flipping its switch back on would take one second, but he does not. He goes home. The frost kills every seedling overnight.
pairs.intended_difference: Marcus actively switches the heater off (A) versus lets a heater that just went off stay off when he could easily restart it (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How seriously did Marcus wrong his neighbor?
pairs.comprehension_question: Just before Marcus decided what to do, what was the state of the heater?
pairs.option_b: It had just switched itself off
pairs.option_c: It had been removed from the greenhouse
pairs.prediction_rationale: Intent and outcome are identical and strongly condemnable, which compresses ratings near the top, so the doing/allowing gap should be present but modest.
pairs.originality_note: Original greenhouse-sabotage scenario with identical malicious motive and ease of action; not the drowning-cousin or similar published doing/allowing pairs.

pairs.title: Booked room
pairs.version_a: At 2 p.m. Nia needs to find her colleague Hana. She opens the office booking system, which is almost always accurate, and sees that Hana booked Room 4 from 2 to 3. Nia concludes that Hana is in Room 4. Hana booked Room 4 on purpose and is sitting in it.
pairs.version_b: At 2 p.m. Nia needs to find her colleague Hana. She opens the office booking system, which is almost always accurate, and sees that Hana booked Room 4 from 2 to 3. pairs.intended_difference: Nia's true, well-supported belief is true because the booking matches Hana's real plan (A) versus only by coincidence after a mistaken booking and a flood (B); Nia's evidence is identical.
pairs.judgment_question: How well does Nia know that Hana is in Room 4?
pairs.scale_label_1: She does not know it at all
pairs.comprehension_question: How did Hana end up in Room 4?

pairs.option_c: Nia asked her to go there
pairs.prediction_rationale: The coincidence in B is vivid and explicit, and models tend to withhold full knowledge when the match with the evidence is accidental.
pairs.originality_note: Original office-booking luck case; the mistaken booking plus flood coincidence is not drawn from any known Gettier or fake-barn vignette.

pairs.title: Cracked rung

pairs.version_b: Elena has an old wooden ladder with a cracked rung. She knows that about one time in twenty a cracked rung gives way. Her neighbor asks to borrow it to paint his fence. pairs.intended_difference: Same choice and known risk; the rung holds (A) or breaks causing injury (B), by chance.
pairs.judgment_question: How much blame does Elena deserve for what she did?

pairs.option_c: No, she did not know about it
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers usually say they judge the choice not the outcome, but a broken arm raises blame somewhat; I expect a modest gap rather than a large one.
pairs.originality_note: Original ladder-lending scenario with an explicit 1-in-20 risk; not a drunk-driver or similar standard moral-luck case.

pairs.title: Ferry rope release
pairs.version_a: Tomas runs the 7:10 ferry out of Pell Harbor. On Tuesday morning Mrs. Ilse Vane was walking up the boarding ramp with a heavy bag when Tomas radioed the dockhand to release the forward rope early. Mrs. Vane had testified against his brother, and for a month he had planned to see her hurt. He felt satisfied watching her fall.
pairs.version_b: Tomas runs the 7:10 ferry out of Pell Harbor. On Tuesday morning Mrs. Ilse Vane was walking up the boarding ramp with a heavy bag when Tomas radioed the dockhand to release the forward rope early. pairs.intended_difference: In A Tomas wants Mrs. Vane hurt and has planned it; in B he has no wish to hurt her. The act, the outcome, and his knowledge that she is on the ramp are identical.

pairs.option_c: Lower the boarding ramp

pairs.title: Acid vent toggle

pairs.version_b: Owen runs the control panel at a chemical plant. Pressure in tank 4 is climbing and must come down before the seals fail. One button on his panel toggles the tank's vent. pairs.option_c: Repairing the tank

pairs.originality_note: Chemical plant vent with a toggle button; built so the effort, knowledge and wants match across the pair. Not a known case, though the doing/allowing shape is general.

pairs.version_b: Priya manages a warehouse. Each morning she needs to know whether the crate of glass lenses has come in from the supplier. pairs.originality_note: Risk: the structure of a true belief from a source that is right by chance is close to the general luck pattern of well-known Gettier-type cases. The warehouse scanner setting is new, but the mechanism is not, so this pair may be judged a re-skin.

pairs.title: Rogue wave hatch
pairs.version_a: Captain Ruiz runs a small trawler back to harbor in a moderate swell. The cargo hatch seal is worn, and he knows a heavy wave could flood the hold. He decides to leave the hatch unlatched for the final ten minutes to save time before the tide turns. The crew is asleep below, and he judges the swell manageable. Ten minutes later, the trawler rounds the breakwater. The swell stays moderate, and the hatch stays dry. The catch arrives in good condition, and the crew are paid as usual.
pairs.version_b: Captain Ruiz runs a small trawler back to harbor in a moderate swell. The cargo hatch seal is worn, and he knows a heavy wave could flood the hold. Ten minutes later, the trawler rounds the breakwater. A rogue wave breaks over the stern, floods the hold, and ruins the whole catch. The crew loses a month's pay.
pairs.intended_difference: Same decision, same knowledge of the risk, same ten minutes. Only the uncontrolled wave differs, so the harmful outcome happens in B and not in A.

pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers tend to rate the same decision as more wrong when it turns out badly, and the lost month's pay is a strong cue. I expect B to be at least 1.5 points higher.
pairs.originality_note: A trawler with a worn hatch seal and a decision to save time; not a known case. The wave is a concrete uncontrolled event rather than a stock example.

pairs.title: Farm gate
pairs.version_a: A public footpath crosses a sheep farm. Where the path leaves the field there is a metal gate with a sign: 'Sheep in field. Walkers must shut this gate behind them.' Shutting the gate would have taken him a few seconds, but he did not want to bother. Nobody else used the path that day. An hour later the sheep had wandered through the gate onto a nearby road. The farmer spent the whole afternoon rounding them up, and one sheep was hit by a car and killed.

Nobody else used the path that day. An hour later the sheep had wandered through the gate onto a nearby road. pairs.judgment_question: How much blame does Daniel deserve for what happened to the sheep?
pairs.comprehension_question: According to the scenario, what state was the gate in when Daniel came up to it?
pairs.option_b: It was already wide open
pairs.option_c: It was missing, leaving only a gap in the fence
pairs.prediction_rationale: His knowledge, motive, the sign's instruction and the few-second cost are the same in both versions, so the failure to shut the gate will still draw heavy blame. I expect about one point more when he opened it himself (about 6.3 versus 5.2).
pairs.originality_note: Not a rescue or sacrifice dilemma: an everyday farm-gate case in which the allowing version has a non-human cause (wind), so no second wrongdoer absorbs the blame.

pairs.title: Parcel tracking
pairs.version_a: Omar was at work, waiting for a parcel to be delivered to his house. At 3:00 pm he opened the courier's tracking page. It said: 'Delivered at 2:14 pm. Left on front porch.' Omar had used this courier for years, and in his experience its tracking page had always been right. He believed that his parcel was on his front porch. In fact, at 2:14 the driver had carried the parcel up to Omar's house, set it down on his front porch, and scanned it as delivered. Nobody had touched it since then, and it was still lying exactly where the driver had put it. So when Omar read the tracking page at 3:00 pm, the parcel really was on his front porch.
pairs.version_b: Omar was at work, waiting for a parcel to be delivered to his house. At 3:00 pm he opened the courier's tracking page. It said: 'Delivered at 2:14 pm. Left on front porch.' Omar had used this courier for years, and in his experience its tracking page had always been right. He believed that his parcel was on his front porch. In fact, at 2:14 the driver had left the parcel on the porch of the wrong house, three streets away, and scanned it as delivered. At 2:40 a stranger living there noticed the label, carried the parcel to Omar's house, and set it down on his front porch. So when Omar read the tracking page at 3:00 pm, the parcel really was on his front porch.
pairs.intended_difference: In A the parcel is on Omar's porch because the driver delivered it there as the tracking page says; in B the driver left it at the wrong house and it is on Omar's porch only because a stranger happened to carry it over.
pairs.judgment_question: When Omar read the tracking page at 3:00 pm, did he know that his parcel was on his front porch?
pairs.comprehension_question: According to the scenario, where did the driver leave the parcel at 2:14 pm?
pairs.option_b: On the porch of a different house
pairs.option_c: At the courier's depot
pairs.prediction_rationale: When the tracking page is right for the ordinary reason, readers will say he knew (6 to 7). When the delivery scan was false and a stranger's later act made the belief true, most will say he did not really know (2 to 3).
pairs.originality_note: The luck comes from a false delivery scan that a stranger's later good deed happens to make true, a mechanism not taken from the stopped-clock, fake-barn, job-and-coins or replaced-object cases.

pairs.title: Garden fire
pairs.version_a: Petra had a large pile of dry branches to get rid of. On Friday afternoon she decided to burn it at the back of her garden, about five metres from the fence she shares with her neighbour, Mr. Lund. She noticed that the wind was picking up, and she knew that sparks can travel in wind. But she wanted the job finished before the weekend, so she lit the pile and stood beside it holding a garden hose. Ten minutes later a sudden strong gust lifted a shower of sparks over the fence before she could do anything. The sparks came down on the gravel path beside Mr. Lund's wooden shed and went out within seconds. Nothing on Mr. Lund's property was damaged.
pairs.version_b: Petra had a large pile of dry branches to get rid of. On Friday afternoon she decided to burn it at the back of her garden, about five metres from the fence she shares with her neighbour, Mr. Lund. She noticed that the wind was picking up, and she knew that sparks can travel in wind. But she wanted the job finished before the weekend, so she lit the pile and stood beside it holding a garden hose. Ten minutes later a sudden strong gust lifted a shower of sparks over the fence before she could do anything. The sparks came down on the roof of Mr. Lund's wooden shed, which caught fire within seconds. The shed and all the tools inside it were destroyed.
pairs.intended_difference: The same gust carries the same sparks over the fence in both versions; in A they land on gravel and die out harmlessly, in B they land on the shed roof and the shed and tools are destroyed.
pairs.judgment_question: How much blame does Petra deserve?
pairs.comprehension_question: According to the scenario, where did the sparks come down?
pairs.option_a: On the gravel path beside the shed
pairs.option_b: On the roof of the shed
pairs.option_c: In Petra's own garden
pairs.prediction_rationale: The decision, her knowledge and the gust are identical, but blame follows the result: mild carelessness when the sparks die on gravel (about 3), serious blame when the shed burns down (about 5.5).
pairs.originality_note: Avoids the driving and child-safety cases used in the moral luck literature; the gust and the sparks crossing the fence occur in both versions and only the landing spot differs.

pairs.title: Storage shelf
pairs.version_a: The storage room of a community centre has one long wooden shelf, used for boxes. A notice fixed to the shelf says: 'For the choir only.' On Monday, Tessa, who belongs to the chess club, put a box of chess clocks on the shelf. The same day, Henrik, who belongs to the choir, put a box of songbooks on the shelf. Each box weighed twenty kilograms. The shelf was strong enough to hold either box by itself, but not both together. Neither Tessa nor Henrik knew this. During the night the shelf gave way under the weight of the two boxes and fell onto a table below, smashing a set of ceramic bowls made by the pottery class.
pairs.version_b: The storage room of a community centre has one long wooden shelf, used for boxes. A notice fixed to the shelf says: 'For the choir and the chess club.' On Monday, Tessa, who belongs to the chess club, put a box of chess clocks on the shelf. The same day, Henrik, who belongs to the choir, put a box of songbooks on the shelf. Each box weighed twenty kilograms. The shelf was strong enough to hold either box by itself, but not both together. Neither Tessa nor Henrik knew this. During the night the shelf gave way under the weight of the two boxes and fell onto a table below, smashing a set of ceramic bowls made by the pottery class.
pairs.intended_difference: The notice on the shelf says 'For the choir only' in A, so Tessa's box was not allowed there, and 'For the choir and the chess club' in B, so it was allowed; nothing else changes.
pairs.judgment_question: How much did Tessa cause the shelf to collapse?
pairs.comprehension_question: According to the notice in the scenario, who was the shelf for?
pairs.option_b: The choir and the chess club
pairs.option_c: The pottery class only
pairs.prediction_rationale: With equal weights, readers will give an even-share answer near 4 when both boxes were allowed and move about one point up when Tessa's box was not supposed to be there. Some readers will hold to the physical half-share, which should keep the gap below 1.5.
pairs.originality_note: It uses the two-person joint-cause design common in work on this topic, but with a new mechanism (equal weights on a shelf) and a rule unrelated to the risk, changed only by the wording of one notice; it is not the pens, computer-login or garden-chemical case.
